name: Papeete Market
label: Papeete Market
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7132559: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The city's main covered market, with flowers, pearls, crafts and food stalls.

text.description:
Papeete Market, known locally as Marché Papeete or the municipal market, is a large market place in Papeete, the capital of Tahiti. It is a good place to photograph because the subjects are close at hand and full of colour: piles of fruit and vegetables, fish, oils, and stalls of handicrafts such as hats and handbags. Vendors also sell local textiles and handcrafted items like shell necklaces, so you can fill a whole set of pictures with small details as well as wider scenes.

Use that spot for a first wide picture of the market and the activity around it, then walk in and look for details. Textiles and necklaces make cheerful close-ups, and a row of stalls gives a strong sense of the place.

Inside, the light can be mixed and the aisles can be busy, so work calmly and keep your phone steady against your body as you shoot. If a stallholder is the main subject of a picture, ask first and be ready to buy a small souvenir or simply say thank you. Check locally before you go for current opening arrangements.
text.geographic_location: Papeete Market is in Papeete, the capital of Tahiti.
text.directions_text: Head for Papeete, the capital of Tahiti. From there the market is 11 m to the north-west, so it is under a minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 10 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for general views of the market and its stalls. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for a more spacious view of the entrance or a busy aisle, and use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as shell necklaces or fruit.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 10 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. From here you can take a first wide shot before going closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place a line of stalls or a doorway along one of the lines for a tidy composition. For close-ups, fill the frame with one type of goods, such as bright fruit or a row of textiles, and keep other stalls soft in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on your main subject, then slide the exposure control down slightly if bright areas look too pale. Portrait mode works well on stalls and products when nobody is directly in the frame; keep it away from people unless they have agreed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to be the liveliest time, with the most stalls busy. Check locally before you go for current times.

text.access_note: This is a public market; check locally before you go for current opening arrangements.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning is probably the busiest and liveliest time at the market.
Lighting inside the market can be mixed, and aisles can be crowded.
It is polite to ask a stallholder before photographing them closely.

name: Papeete Tahiti Temple
label: Tahiti Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Papeete Tahiti Temple' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/734682036: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Papeete Tahiti Temple' (57 m across).
notes: A white temple on the hillside east of the city centre.

text.description: The Papeete Tahiti Temple is a temple of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and it makes a neat, colourful photo stop. White walls, a blue tile roof and a single slender spire topped with a gold angel Moroni statue stand out against the tropical greenery and sky. The walls are stucco mixed with imported white sand, and the spire is about 66 feet (around 20 metres) tall. The design blends French and Polynesian touches. The temple was first dedicated in October 1983, then closed in 2005 for a major renovation and rededicated in November 2006. In 2009 the church bought the neighbouring land and added gardens, parking and a straightened access road, which means the building can now be seen from the street much more easily. That is good news for photographers, because the front view is the one to go for: the facade, with the flags and gardens in front and the spire rising behind. The grounds are described as open to visitors, with winding paths and neat gardens that frame the building. Take a wide shot first to show the whole temple, then move in for details such as the roof, the spire and the statue. Look for a clear patch of sky, as the white walls can look harsh in strong midday sun. Please keep to the paths, and be aware that taking photographs inside the temple is not allowed.
text.geographic_location: The temple stands in the commune of Pirae, just outside central Papeete, on the main-road side with its entrance and gardens. Its grounds sit next to a church meetinghouse.
text.directions_text: No tram or bus stops are listed for this spot. The temple is in the commune of Pirae, so check a map or ask locally for current ways of getting there. Once there, walk into the front gardens on the main-road side, where the phone icon on the map is. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade with the gardens and flags in front. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the spire will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the spire and the gold statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the temple's front facade fills the view, with the gardens and flags in the foreground, the blue roof, and the single spire topped by the gold Angel Moroni statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the spire on one of the vertical lines, keeping the building level. Use the flags or garden plants as a foreground layer to add depth. Hold the phone upright for the full height of the spire, then turn it sideways for a wider shot of the frontage. Tilting the phone up from close by will make the building lean back, so step back a little if you can and zoom in instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the walls keep their detail and the sky stays blue. For the gold statue, zoom in, tap on it and check that it is not washed out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when guides recommend going for better light and quieter grounds.

text.access_note: The grounds are described as open to visitors, but only church members with a current temple recommend can enter the temple itself and photography inside is not allowed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Parc Bougainville
label: Parc Bougainville
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenue du Général de Gaulle' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Avenue du Général de Gaulle nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W500293070 (Parc Bougainville): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Shaded city park with monuments in front of the Assembly.

text.description:
Parc Bougainville is a green park in the middle of Papeete, set directly across the avenue from the waterfront. It photographs well because the trees along the avenue form a natural frame around the park's edge, and the harbour is just behind you. Inside, the bronze bust of the navigator stands at the entrance, with the park's trees and cannons around it. That makes a good close-up with a bit of character. The lawns and trees are also a pleasant foreground if you come near sunset, when the sky can add colour behind them.

For an easy first picture, stand on Avenue du Général de Gaulle on the waterfront side and shoot across to the park's edge. Let the tree trunks and branches make a loose border, and keep the road low in the picture so the green is what you notice. Then cross over and go in for the bust and the cannons, which suit a tighter, more detailed shot.

A small warning: some areas of the park are a little worn, and it may look less tidy in person than in glossy photos. Frame to leave out bare patches and bins, and you'll get a calmer picture. Take care when standing near the avenue and watch for traffic.
text.geographic_location: In central Papeete, in the town-centre waterfront area. The park lies directly across Avenue du Général de Gaulle from the harbour front.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed nearby. From there, the park is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the park's edge framed by the trees. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you can't step back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the bronze bust and the cannons.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Avenue du Général de Gaulle (waterfront side, directly opposite the park). The park's edge framed by the trees along the avenue, with the harbour side behind the photographer. On the waterfront side, directly opposite the park. From here the park lies to the north-west, and the harbour is behind you. You see the park's edge framed by the trees along the avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line of the park's edge on the lower third. Let the trees along the avenue fill the sides and top as a frame. For a different view, go into the park and photograph the bronze bust at the entrance with the trees and cannons around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the trees or the bust to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the greens stay rich and the sky doesn't burn out. Use portrait mode on the bust if you want the background softly blurred.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon towards sunset, when the lawns and trees can have the sky colours behind them. Earlier in the day is better for a plain, clear shot of the bust.

text.access_note: Parc Bougainville is a public park, but check the official site before you go for any access restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon and sunset light can add colour to the sky behind the park.
Parts of the park are worn and it can look less tidy than in photos.
The pavement along Avenue du Général de Gaulle may be narrow in places and the avenue has traffic.
The ultra-wide lens helps if you cannot step back from the park's edge.

name: Paofai Gardens
label: Paofai Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenue Pouvana'a a Oopa' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Avenue Pouvanaa a Oopa' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OSM R10021353 (Paofai): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Waterfront gardens with views across to Moorea.

text.description: Paofai Gardens is a green park on Papeete's waterfront, with palm trees, lawns, ponds and a paved walkway along the lagoon edge. It suits a phone because it gives you several kinds of picture in one walk. The seafront promenade is the classic approach. On one side are the gardens and palms, and on the other is the open harbour with Moorea in the distance. Passing ferries make a good moving backdrop to the island. Inside the park, the ponds hold koi and aquatic plants, and the palms and greenery frame them nicely at close and middle range. Statues and memorials stand against the lawns, which gives you a more cultural picture of the place. Be aware that the harbour side can also show shipping docks and a cargo yard, which can spoil a frame. Point your phone toward Moorea and away from the port, and the picture stays calm and tropical. Late afternoon is recommended for the seascape, when the light turns soft and warm. Take a few steps back from the railing or kerb so the palms form a line leading into the picture. Playgrounds have reportedly been closed at times, so don't plan a picture around them.
text.geographic_location: Paofai Gardens lies in the Paofai area of Papeete, along the lagoon edge of the town. The waterfront promenade is Avenue Pouvana'a a Oopa, with the harbour on the seaward side.
text.directions_text: From central Papeete, head to Avenue Pouvana'a a Oopa and start. Keep the lagoon on your side and walk along the palm-lined promenade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the promenade and the palms. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole walkway with the sky. Use 2x or more, if your phone has it, to bring Moorea and the ferries closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Avenue Pouvana'a a Oopa (waterfront promenade along the lagoon edge of the gardens, looking out toward Moorea). Palm-lined paved walkway with the gardens on one side and the open harbour, shipping docks and Moorea in the distance on the other. On the waterfront promenade along the lagoon edge of the gardens. You will see the palm-lined paved walkway with the gardens on one side and the harbour and Moorea on the other.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn your phone toward Moorea and keep the docks and cargo yard out of the frame. Turn on the gridlines and put the line of palms on one third of the frame, with the lagoon and Moorea on the other. For a different picture, go into the park for close and middle shots of the koi ponds, or for the statues and memorials against the lawns.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sea or Moorea to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the palms don't turn flat. Try a Live Photo when a ferry passes. Wipe the lens first, as sea air can leave a haze on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light is soft and warm.

text.access_note: The gardens are a public seafront park, but check the official site before you go for opening times and any closed areas such as playgrounds.
claims_not_in_sources: Sea air can leave a haze or film on a phone lens.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep the sky blue and stops palms and sky from looking washed out.
Gridlines and a line of palms help the viewer's eye lead into the picture.

name: Mairie de Papeete
label: Papeete Town Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rue des Remparts' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Rue des Remparts nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM N8117580518 (Mairie de Papeete): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The town hall, modelled on the former royal palace of Queen Pomare.

text.description: The Mairie de Papeete is the town hall, a yellow building with a colonial-style front, set in grounds with tropical trees. That mix of warm colour and green foliage makes it an easy, pleasant subject for a phone. The simplest picture is a street-level view from Rue des Remparts, where the building sits behind its garden and the trees can frame it naturally. Keep the trees in the foreground and let the yellow walls fill the middle of the frame. Switch on the gridlines and line the front up with them so the building looks straight. If the whole front won't fit, step back along the pavement rather than tilting the phone upwards, which makes the walls lean. Wait for a gap in passing people if you want a clean shot. A second option is a closer view of the front of the building itself, which shows the colonial-style yellow front best in soft morning light. Take a wide shot first, then move in and photograph a detail such as a doorway, a window or the tree shadows on the wall. Treat it as a quick, easy stop. It is worth a few minutes and a handful of frames rather than a long session. As ever, be considerate of other people around you.
text.geographic_location: The Mairie de Papeete is in central Papeete. The exact address is given as either Rue des Remparts or Avenue du Général de Gaulle, so check on the day. Rue des Remparts works well as a street-level viewpoint.
text.directions_text: There are no train or tram stops for this spot, which is in central Papeete. The town hall is to the south-west of it, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full front with the trees in front. If you are close and the building will not fit, use the ultra-wide (0.5x), keeping the phone level. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as windows and the front doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rue des Remparts (street-level view of the building's facade). The town hall framed from the street, with its grounds and tropical trees in the foreground. From here the town hall can be framed from the street, with its grounds and tropical trees in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the building's vertical edges parallel to the vertical lines. Let the tree branches and garden fill the bottom or one side of the frame. For an alternative, walk to the front of the town hall itself for a straight-on shot of the yellow colonial-style front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the yellow wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Take one shot at 1x and one at 0.5x so you can choose later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning light suits the yellow front of the building best.

text.access_note: Photograph from the street and be considerate of other people around you.
claims_not_in_sources: Strong midday tropical sun can wash out a bright yellow wall, so lowering the exposure slider helps.
The building can be photographed from the street without going inside.
Tilting the phone upwards makes the building's walls appear to lean.

name: Papeete Cathedral
label: Papeete Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parc Bougainville' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parc Bougainville' (way/500293070): middle (121 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/32774088: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Papeete' (50 m across).
notes: The white Catholic cathedral of Notre-Dame de l'Immaculée Conception.

text.description: Papeete Cathedral is the main Catholic church in Tahiti's capital, dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception and named after Notre Dame de Paris. It opened in 1875 and is the oldest Catholic church on the island. It is also one of the few early colonial buildings left in central Papeete. The building has a yellow facade with pointed-arch windows, and a hexagonal bell tower topped with a red spire. That spire sits over the entrance and faces towards Mont Aorai. The colours stand out well against green leaves and a tropical sky, which is why it works so well on a phone screen. Inside, the design mixes European and Polynesian touches. One example is a full-size carving of the Madonna and Child from the Marquesas Islands, where the child holds a breadfruit. The best-known view is straight on from the square in front. For something calmer, try Parc Bougainville, a short walk to the west. From there the whole building can be framed by trees, which gives a softer, more spacious picture than the facade alone. Allow a few minutes to move around the building, because a small change of position can lose or gain the red spire against the sky. If you step inside, remember it is a working church, so keep your phone quiet and respectful.
text.geographic_location: In central Papeete on Tahiti, on the rue du Général de Gaulle, close to the waterfront esplanade. Parc Bougainville, the suggested viewpoint, lies a short walk to the west.
text.directions_text: There are no listed public transport stops to start from, so head on foot from the central waterfront esplanade area of Papeete to Parc Bougainville. From the park, the cathedral is to the east, about 5 minutes on foot. The cathedral is on the rue du Général de Gaulle, close to the waterfront. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole building and the trees around it, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the red spire and the bell tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parc Bougainville. A wide-angle view of the cathedral building framed by lush greenery. From here you see the cathedral building as a wide view, framed by lush greenery, with the cathedral to the east. It is a quieter spot than the front of the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the walls and bell tower upright by holding the phone level. Let branches and leaves form the edges of the picture and place the cathedral in the middle. For the classic close view of the yellow facade, pointed windows and red spire, walk over to Place de la Cathédrale. Rue Jeanne d'Arc is another option for a view along the street, but check what it looks like now.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the yellow wall to focus. If the sky is washing out, drag the exposure slider down a little so the red spire and the sky keep their colour.

text.access_note: Parc Bougainville is a public park, but check the official site before you go for its current opening state; the cathedral is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and dress expectations.
claims_not_in_sources: The cathedral is a working church, so visitors should be quiet and respectful inside, and visiting times or dress expectations may apply.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep colour in the red spire against a bright sky.
Using the ultra-wide lens up close can slightly stretch the edges of a building, so keep the phone level.

name: Maison James Norman Hall
label: James Norman Hall Hous
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/676707956: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Musée James Norman Hall' (30 m across).
notes: Seaside home of the author of Mutiny on the Bounty, in Arue, now a small museum.

text.description:
Maison James Norman Hall is the former home of the writer James Norman Hall, now a small house museum. Hall settled in Tahiti in 1924 and built the house himself in 1926. Between 1932 and 1934 he co-wrote the three volumes of The Bounty Trilogy here. He died in 1951, and the house is shown as it was then. Inside are his 3,000-volume library and his typewriter, along with personal items lent by the Hall family. The house fell into ruin after his wife died in 1985. It was restored with help from his daughter Nancy and opened as a museum on 17 January 2002.

For photographs, the appeal is the setting more than the building. One visiting writer described a hilltop spot with a verandah, tall palms and frangipani, and the house sits in that garden. Think of a modest, practical home surrounded by greenery, not a grand monument. That suits a phone well: you can show the whole house with its plants around it, then move closer for small details such as the verandah, shutters and flowers.

Take a few steps to either side to find a clear view between the plants. Check the official site before you go to confirm whether the house and grounds are open and whether photography is allowed inside.
text.geographic_location: The house is in Arue, on the island of Tahiti, on a hillside plot with a garden. Papeete is the nearest main town on this map.
text.directions_text: No tram or Underground-style stops are listed for this spot, so from Papeete or the centre of Arue it is easiest to go by taxi or hired scooter. Ask the driver for the Maison James Norman Hall, also called the Musée James Norman Hall. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the house in its garden. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the grounds are tight and you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for verandah and window details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. If plants block the view, shift a few steps sideways rather than zooming in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the house on one third of the frame, with palms and flowering shrubs filling the rest, so the garden setting shows. Keep the phone level so the verandah roof lines stay straight. Then take a closer shot of a flower or part of the verandah with the telephoto lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the house to set focus and drag the exposure slider down slightly if the bright sky turns the walls pale. If the shade is deep, tap on a shadowed wall and lift the exposure a little.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the garden colours look richer. Midday sun can make strong patches of light and shade under the trees.

text.access_note: This is a museum, so it may be ticketed or have set visiting times; check the official site before you go.
